question: Ice is 917 kg per cubic metre. Heat water from freezing to boiling: how light does it get?
answer: Nowhere near ice. Boiling water is 958, only 4% lighter than cold water, so ice floats even in boiling water. Heat jostles water molecules apart; freezing locks them into an open hexagonal lattice that takes 9% more room. That is why frost bursts pipes: freezing swells water twice as much as boiling.
move: When comparing two changes, ask which one rebuilds the structure.
ask: Which change in my life rebuilt how things fit together, rather than just turning them up?

verdict.under: Too light. Even boiling water is 958, far heavier than ice: ice floats in a boiling pan.
verdict.near: Right: heating thins water by only 4%, and it never gets near ice's 917.
verdict.over: Lighter than that: by 100 °C water is 4% thinner, but still far heavier than ice.

reference: Kell, Density, thermal expansivity and compressibility of liquid water from 0 to 150 °C, Journal of Chemical and Engineering Data 20:97-105, 1975; Hobbs, Ice Physics, Clarendon Press, 1974 (ice at 0 °C: 916.7 kg per cubic metre)
